title: Idols on Trial, Israel Reassured
overview: God puts the nations and their idols on trial, claims to be the one steering history through a coming conqueror, and promises frightened Israel help and care.

parts.label: Nations called to court (vv. 1-4)
parts.note: God summons faraway nations to a trial and asks who has raised up a conqueror from the east who sweeps through kingdoms. Most scholars see Cyrus, the Persian king named later in Isaiah (44:28, 45:1), and the answer given is that the LORD, first and last, stands behind history.

parts.label: Nations scramble for idols (vv. 5-7)
parts.note: Afraid of the conqueror, the nations cheer each other on and rush to build new idols, nailing them down so they will not tip over. The scene is quietly mocking: a god that must be nailed in place cannot hold anyone else up.

parts.label: Israel is not abandoned (vv. 8-13)
parts.note: Speaking most likely to Jewish exiles in Babylon, God calls Israel a chosen servant, the family of Abraham, God's friend, and says they have not been thrown away. Holding their right hand pictures a close, steadying grip, and their enemies will vanish without a trace.

parts.label: From worm to threshing sledge (vv. 14-16)
parts.note: "Worm" names how small and trampled the exiles felt, and "Redeemer" meant a relative who bought back a family member from debt or slavery. A threshing sledge was a heavy board with sharp teeth dragged over grain, so weak Israel is pictured crushing "mountains," probably meaning powerful hostile nations.

parts.label: Rivers in the desert (vv. 17-20)
parts.note: God promises the thirsty poor, most likely the exiles, rivers, springs and shade trees in dry land, echoing Israel's desert journey after Egypt. Whether this pictures a road home or something larger is open, but the stated aim is that everyone will see God did it.

parts.label: Idols put on trial (vv. 21-29)
parts.note: God dares the idols to explain the past, predict the future, or do anything at all, and the harsh verdict is that they are nothing and choosing them is detestable. God claims to have announced the conqueror (from north and east, likely meaning Media and Persia) and to send Jerusalem good news, while the idols are only wind.

disagreement: Most readers take the conqueror from the east as Cyrus, but some older Christian interpreters saw Abraham there, and others read the passage as also pointing ahead to Jesus.
think: When you have felt small and outmatched, what, if anything, gave you a sense of being held steady?
